collection.title: Entrepreneurship: Starting and Running a Small Business

questions.section_skill: Describe a business as solving a problem for paying customers
questions.outcome_title: Describe a business as solving a problem for customers who pay, and tell revenue-seeking activity from a hobby
questions.intro: A business sells something people want: a service, a product, a digital file, or content. An entrepreneur is a person who starts and runs a business and takes on its risk. The key test is simple: does it solve a problem or meet a want for customers who are willing to pay? A hobby is done mainly for enjoyment; it may sell sometimes, but it is not organized to earn money. A business plans to earn more than it spends over time, even if it starts small.
questions.prompt: Dana bakes bread for fun and gives it to friends. Which change would turn this into a business?

choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
She posts photos of her bread online each day.
She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.

questions.correct_answer: She starts selling loaves each week to neighbors who pay for them.
questions.feedback: A business needs customers who pay. Selling loaves to neighbors who pay is the change that matters.

wrong_choices.text: She buys a bigger, more expensive oven so she can bake more loaves at once.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: buying equipment alone does not create customers

wrong_choices.text: She posts photos of her bread online each day.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: posting photos does not involve customers paying

wrong_choices.text: She bakes twice as many loaves to give away.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: giving more away is still not selling to customers

questions.section_skill: Compare a side business and a full-time business
questions.outcome_title: Compare a side business with a full-time business by time, income needs and risk
questions.intro: A side business runs alongside a job or school. A full-time business is your main work and main income. A side business usually has less risk, because a paycheck or other income still covers living costs while you test the idea, but it has less time. A full-time business has more time but more risk: if sales are slow, personal bills may go unpaid. Many owners start on the side, then decide later using evidence such as steady sales, savings and a clear plan.
questions.prompt: Mia works 40 hours a week and wants to test a pet-sitting idea. Which plan has the lower personal risk?

choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
Sign a long lease for a pet store
Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
Quit her job today to pet-sit full time

questions.correct_answer: Keep her job and pet-sit on weekends to test demand
questions.feedback: Keeping her job while testing keeps her bills covered, so the personal risk is lower.

wrong_choices.text: Borrow money to open a large pet hotel later this month
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a large loan adds risk before demand is known

wrong_choices.text: Sign a long lease for a pet store
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a lease is a big commitment before testing

wrong_choices.text: Quit her job today to pet-sit full time
wrong_choices.why_wrong: this removes her steady income before the idea is tested

questions.intro: An offer (also called a value proposition) says, in plain words, who it is for, what problem it solves, and what result the customer gets. A simple pattern: "For [customer] who [problem], we [what you do] so you can [result]." For example: "For busy pet owners who work late, we walk your dog at lunch so it gets exercise and you do not rush home." A clear offer is specific, honest and easy to repeat. It avoids vague phrases like "best quality" that do not say what the customer gets.

questions.section_skill: Tell the paying customer from the user and the decision-maker
questions.outcome_title: Tell the paying customer from the user and the decision-maker
questions.intro: The CUSTOMER is the person or organization who pays. The USER is the person who uses the product or service. Sometimes they are the same; sometimes they are different. A parent pays for a child's piano lessons; the child is the user. A company pays for software its workers use. There may also be a DECISION-MAKER who chooses, like a manager who approves a purchase. To sell well, you must convince whoever pays and decides, while also making the product work for the user.

questions.intro: A leading question pushes a person toward a particular answer. "Don't you hate waiting for the bus?" pushes toward yes. A neutral question lets the person answer honestly: "How do you usually get to work?" or "What, if anything, bothers you about your commute?" Leading questions make an idea look better than it is. Neutral questions, about real experience, make the results trustworthy.

questions.section_skill: Identify competitors and other alternatives
questions.outcome_title: Identify direct competitors and the other ways customers solve the problem today
questions.intro: Competitors are businesses selling something similar to the same customers. Alternatives are any other way customers solve the problem today, including doing it themselves, using a free tool, or doing nothing. A lawn-care business competes with other lawn services, but also with homeowners who mow their own lawns. Studying competitors and alternatives shows what customers already accept, what they pay, and what they complain about. "No competition" usually means you have not looked hard enough, or that few people want it.

questions.set_title: Likes and praise are not demand
questions.section_skill: Explain why likes and praise are weak demand signals
questions.outcome_title: Explain why likes, follows and compliments are weak demand signals
questions.intro: Likes, follows, views and compliments feel good, but they are weak signs of demand. They cost people nothing, so many people give them freely. A post with 2,000 likes may lead to zero sales. Followers can also be people who enjoy your content but will never buy, or accounts that are not real people. To judge demand, look for actions that cost the person something: purchases, deposits, bookings, or replies asking how to buy. Treat likes as a sign of attention, not of buying.

Demand is very strong because of the likes.
Likes and sales always move together.

questions.feedback: Attention is not the same as buying.

wrong_choices.text: The likes prove sales will rise soon.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: likes do not predict sales reliably

wrong_choices.text: Demand is very strong because of the likes.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: likes did not turn into sales

wrong_choices.text: Likes and sales always move together.
wrong_choices.why_wrong: this example shows they do not

questions.intro: Checking a name is not the same as owning it. A domain name you can buy, a social media handle that is free, or a state's approval of an LLC name only shows that THAT specific spot was available. It does not give trademark rights, and it does not mean the name is safe to use. Another business may already use the same or a similar name for similar goods or services, and could object. Before investing in a name, also search for businesses using it and consider a trademark search (US: the USPTO database). Rules: US, check current guidance.

questions.intro: A SOLE PROPRIETORSHIP is one person doing business without forming a separate entity. It is the default: if you sell on your own and do not register another form, you are usually a sole proprietor. It is simple, but the business is not separate from you, so you are personally responsible for its debts. A GENERAL PARTNERSHIP is two or more people doing business together for profit without forming another entity. Partners usually share profits and can each be personally responsible for business debts. Source: SBA guidance; state law varies.

questions.intro: A LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY (LLC) is a business entity formed by filing with a state. Its main feature is limited liability: generally, business debts and lawsuits are the company's, not the owners' personal ones. A CORPORATION is also formed with the state; it is owned by shareholders and run with more formal rules. Both can help separate personal and business risk, but neither is total immunity: owners can still be personally responsible for their own wrongful acts, for personal guarantees they sign, or if they mix personal and business money. Source: SBA; state law varies.

questions.intro: Forming an LLC, at a basic level: (1) choose a name that the state will accept; (2) name a registered agent, a person or company with a physical address in the state who accepts official legal papers for the business during business hours; (3) file formation papers (often called articles of organization) with the state and pay the fee; (4) write an operating agreement; (5) then handle tax IDs, licenses and a bank account. questions.intro: Forming an LLC, at a basic level: (1) choose a name that the state will accept; (2) name a registered agent, a person or company with a physical address in the state who accepts official legal papers for the business during business hours; (3) file formation papers (often called articles of organization) with the state and pay the fee; (4) write an operating agreement; (5) then handle tax IDs, licenses and a bank account. questions.section_skill: Identify what an operating agreement should cover
questions.outcome_title: Identify what a written agreement among owners should cover
questions.intro: An operating agreement is a written document among an LLC's owners (members) that sets the rules for running the business. It usually covers: who owns what percentage; who makes which decisions; how profits and losses are shared; what happens if an owner wants to leave, becomes unable to work, or dies; how new owners can join; and how disagreements are settled. Even a one-owner LLC can benefit from one. Some states require it. Writing it while everyone gets along prevents painful arguments later.

questions.section_skill: Explain what a DBA does and does not do
questions.outcome_title: Explain when a trade name (DBA) filing is used and what it does not do
questions.intro: A DBA ("doing business as"), also called a trade name, assumed name or fictitious name, lets a business operate under a name different from its legal name. A sole proprietor named Maria Lopez who sells as "Sunny Bakes" may need to register that name; so may an LLC operating under a different name. Where it is filed (state, county or city) depends on the location. A DBA does NOT create a new entity, does NOT give liability protection, and does NOT give trademark rights. Check local rules.
questions.prompt: Maria Lopez sells cakes as "Sunny Bakes." What does a DBA filing let her do?

choices.text: Turn her business into an LLC without other filings
Stop all others from using "Sunny Bakes" nationwide
Protect her house from business debts

questions.correct_answer: Operate under the name "Sunny Bakes"
questions.feedback: A DBA registers a name the business uses.

wrong_choices.text: Turn her business into an LLC without other filings
wrong_choices.why_wrong: a DBA does not create an entity

wrong_choices.text: Stop all others from using "Sunny Bakes" nationwide
Protect her house from business debts

questions.intro: A DBA ("doing business as"), also called a trade name, assumed name or fictitious name, lets a business operate under a name different from its legal name. questions.section_skill: Recognize personal guarantees and how they bypass limited liability
questions.outcome_title: Recognize how personal guarantees and personal actions can bypass limited liability
questions.intro: Limited liability has gaps. A PERSONAL GUARANTEE is a promise you sign to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot. Lenders, landlords and some suppliers often ask new business owners for one, because the business has little history. If you sign it, your personal savings and other assets can be used to pay that debt, even if you have an LLC. Personal guarantees can be hidden in long forms. Read before signing, ask what you are guaranteeing, and consider whether the amount is one you could pay personally.
questions.prompt: What is a personal guarantee?

choices.text: A promise to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot
A promise by the bank to lend you more money later
A guarantee that the business will make a profit this year
A warranty you give customers on a product

questions.correct_answer: A promise to pay a business debt yourself if the business cannot
questions.feedback: It makes you personally responsible for that debt.

wrong_choices.text: A promise by the bank to lend you more money later
A guarantee that the business will make a profit this year
A warranty you give customers on a product

questions.section_skill: Explain what an EIN is and who usually needs one
questions.outcome_title: Explain what an Employer Identification Number (EIN) is for and when to check whether one is needed
questions.intro: An EIN (Employer Identification Number) is a nine-digit number the IRS (the federal tax agency) gives a business to identify it for federal taxes, much like a Social Security number identifies a person. Businesses that hire employees, most partnerships and corporations, and many LLCs need one. Banks often ask for it when opening a business account. Even a sole proprietor without employees may choose to get one so she can give clients the EIN instead of her Social Security number. The IRS says an EIN is free: you never have to pay a fee for one.

A federal tax ID number for a business

questions.feedback: The IRS issues EINs to identify businesses for federal taxes.

Even a sole proprietor without employees may choose to get one so she can give clients the EIN instead of her Social Security number. The IRS says an EIN is free: you never have to pay a fee for one.

questions.intro: Different numbers and filings do different jobs. The EIN is the FEDERAL tax ID from the IRS. A STATE tax ID or account may be needed for state taxes, such as collecting sales tax or paying state payroll taxes; it comes from the state's tax agency. BUSINESS REGISTRATION (forming an LLC, or filing a DBA) records the business or its name with the state or local government. A LICENSE gives permission to operate. questions.section_skill: Explain why business money needs its own account
questions.outcome_title: Explain why business money belongs in a separate account
questions.intro: A separate business bank account keeps business money apart from personal money. All business income goes in and all business expenses come out of it. This makes bookkeeping and taxes easier, shows clearly what the business earns, and helps support the separation between an LLC or corporation and its owner. Mixing personal and business money in one account is called COMMINGLING. It makes records confusing and can weaken liability protection. The SBA lists opening a business bank account as a launch step.

Paying taxes on time each quarter

questions.set_title: Moving money between owner and business
questions.section_skill: Record contributions, draws and owner loans correctly
questions.outcome_title: Record owner contributions and owner withdrawals separately from sales and expenses
questions.intro: Owners move money in and out of a business in a few ways. An OWNER CONTRIBUTION is money the owner puts in. An OWNER'S DRAW (also called a distribution) is an owner withdrawal for personal use; for sole proprietors and most LLCs, a draw is not a wage and is not a business expense, so it lowers the business's cash but does not reduce its profit. A LOAN from the owner to the business should be written down with how it will be repaid. In every case, move the money by transfer and record what it is, so the books show the truth.
questions.prompt: Money an owner puts into the business is called what?

choices.text: An owner's draw for personal use
A customer payment for a product

questions.correct_answer: An owner contribution
questions.feedback: A contribution is money in from the owner.

wrong_choices.text: An owner's draw for personal use
A customer payment for a product

questions.section_skill: Reconcile records with the bank statement and explain differences
questions.outcome_title: Match business records against the bank statement and explain differences
questions.intro: RECONCILING means comparing your own records with the bank statement to make sure they match. Each month, check every deposit and withdrawal. Differences usually come from: transactions the bank has not processed yet (such as a check that has not cleared), bank fees you did not record, mistakes in your records, or charges you do not recognize. Unknown charges may be errors or fraud and should be reported to the bank quickly. Reconciling catches problems while they are still small.
questions.prompt: What does reconciling mean?

Paying all bills on the same day
Asking the bank for a loan

questions.section_skill: Classify fixed and variable costs and compute total cost
questions.outcome_title: Classify costs as fixed or variable and use them in a small total
questions.intro: A FIXED cost stays about the same no matter how much you sell in a period: rent, insurance, a software plan. A VARIABLE cost goes up as you sell more: ingredients, packaging, shipping, or payment fees on each sale. Example: a candle maker pays 500 dollars of rent a month (fixed) and 4 dollars of wax and jar for each candle (variable). Making 100 candles costs 500 + 4 x 100 = 900 dollars. Knowing which is which helps you plan prices and see what happens when sales change.

Monthly rent for the bakery building

questions.section_skill: Compute cost per item and compare it with price
questions.outcome_title: Find cost per item and profit per item from a stated price
questions.intro: COST PER ITEM (unit cost) is what it costs you to make or buy one item. If a batch of 40 cookies uses 20 dollars of ingredients and 4 dollars of bags, the cost per cookie is (20 + 4) / 40 = 0.60 dollars. PRICE is what the customer pays. The difference, price minus cost per item, is what each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit. A price below the cost per item loses money on every sale. Include everything the item uses, such as packaging and labels, not just the main material.
questions.prompt: A batch of 50 bracelets uses 75 dollars of beads and string. What is the cost per bracelet?
questions.correct_answer: 1.50 dollars

questions.intro: Three words get mixed up. REVENUE (sales) is all the money earned from customers before costs. PROFIT is revenue minus all expenses for the same period. questions.section_skill: Compute markup and margin and tell them apart
questions.outcome_title: Compute markup and margin and explain why they differ
questions.intro: MARKUP and MARGIN both describe the gap between cost and price, but they use different bases. MARKUP is the gap as a percent of COST: (price - cost) / cost. MARGIN is the gap as a percent of PRICE: (price - cost) / price. Example: cost 6 dollars, price 10 dollars. The gap is 4. Markup = 4 / 6, about 67 percent. Margin = 4 / 10 = 40 percent. For an item with a positive cost sold above cost, the markup percentage is greater than the margin percentage. Mixing them up can lead to prices that are too low.
questions.prompt: Cost 5 dollars, price 8 dollars. What is the markup?
questions.correct_answer: 60 percent

questions.intro: MARKUP and MARGIN both describe the gap between cost and price, but they use different bases. MARKUP is the gap as a percent of COST: (price - cost) / cost. questions.section_skill: Calculate break-even from stated assumptions
questions.outcome_title: Find a break-even quantity from fixed costs and profit per item
questions.intro: The BREAK-EVEN point is the number of sales at which total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero. Each sale contributes (price - variable cost per item) toward fixed costs. Break-even units = fixed costs / (price - variable cost). Example (assumptions): fixed costs 600 dollars a month, price 15 dollars, variable cost 5 dollars: 600 / 10 = 60 sales. Sales above break-even create profit; sales below create a loss. Write down the assumptions; if any change, recalculate. Round UP, because you cannot sell part of an item.
questions.prompt: Fixed costs 800 dollars, price 20 dollars, variable cost 10 dollars. What is break-even?
questions.correct_answer: 80 sales

questions.section_skill: Calculate processing fees and include them in pricing
questions.outcome_title: Include a stated processing fee when finding what a sale brings in
questions.intro: When customers pay by card or app, the payment processor keeps a fee. A common structure is a percentage of the sale plus a fixed amount per transaction, for example (an assumption, not a real quote) 2.9 percent + 0.30 dollars. On a 40-dollar sale that is 0.029 x 40 + 0.30 = 1.46 dollars, so the business receives 38.54 dollars. The fixed part hurts small sales most: on a 3-dollar sale, 0.30 dollars alone is 10 percent. Include fees in cost per sale when setting prices.

questions.section_skill: Compute effective hourly rates and recognize capacity limits
questions.outcome_title: Include the owner's time and limited capacity when judging a price
questions.intro: An owner's time is limited, so it has a cost. CAPACITY is the most work the business can do in a period. If an owner can work 30 hours a week on paid tasks, that is her capacity. To find an effective HOURLY RATE, divide profit from a job by the total hours it takes, including travel, emails, invoices and setup, not just the visible work. A price that looks high can become a low hourly rate. When capacity is full, serving more customers safely takes qualified help or a better process. Raising prices is a separate choice: it manages demand and earns more per job, but it does not add capacity.
questions.prompt: A job earns 120 dollars of profit and takes 4 hours in total. What is the effective hourly rate?
questions.correct_answer: 30 dollars an hour

questions.section_skill: Size and build a business cash reserve
questions.outcome_title: Size a simple cash reserve from stated monthly costs
questions.intro: A CASH RESERVE (emergency fund) is money the business keeps aside for slow months, repairs or late payments. A common planning approach is to save enough to cover a set number of months of essential expenses, such as 2 to 3 months; this is a planning assumption, not a rule. Build it gradually, for example by moving a percentage of each sale into a separate savings account. Use it for planned shortfalls such as slow months and for unexpected needs, then refill it. Without a reserve, one surprise can force expensive borrowing.

questions.section_skill: Keeping a running balance
questions.outcome_title: Record transactions in a simple ledger with sensible categories
questions.intro: A running balance adds money in and subtracts money out, one line at a time. Start with the opening amount. For each line: if money comes in, add; if money goes out, subtract. Example: start 300; +150 = 450; -60 = 390; -40 = 350. Check: opening + total in - total out = 300 + 150 - 100 = 350. Both ways should agree.

questions.set_title: Invoices, bills, money owed to you and by you
questions.section_skill: Track invoices and bills as receivables and payables
questions.outcome_title: Tell invoices from bills and accounts receivable from accounts payable
questions.intro: An INVOICE is a bill YOU send to a customer; until it is paid, it is money owed TO you, called ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE. A BILL from a supplier is money YOU owe, called ACCOUNTS PAYABLE. A good invoice shows your business name, the customer, an invoice number, the date, what was provided, the amount, the due date and how to pay. Track both lists: who owes you, and whom you owe, with due dates. Paying bills on time protects your reputation with suppliers.
questions.prompt: Money customers owe you is called what?
questions.correct_answer: Accounts receivable

questions.section_skill: Record owner contributions, draws and loans without distorting profit
questions.outcome_title: Keep owner money moves out of sales and expenses in the records
questions.intro: In the books, owner money is kept separate from income and expenses. An OWNER CONTRIBUTION increases the owner's stake (called owner's equity) but is NOT sales revenue. An OWNER DRAW decreases owner's equity but is NOT a business expense for a sole proprietor or most LLCs. A LOAN from the owner is recorded as money the business owes back. Mislabeling these makes profit look wrong: a contribution recorded as a sale inflates profit; a draw recorded as an expense hides it.

questions.section_skill: Tell cash basis from accrual basis with a timing example
questions.outcome_title: Tell cash-basis from accrual-basis recording in a simple example
questions.intro: There are two common ways to record when income and expenses count. CASH BASIS records income when money is received and expenses when money is paid. ACCRUAL BASIS records income when it is earned (for example, when the work is done and invoiced) and expenses when they are incurred, even if payment happens later. questions.section_skill: Read the three basic reports and match each to its question
questions.outcome_title: Tell what a profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow summary each show
questions.intro: Three common reports summarize the books. A PROFIT AND LOSS statement (P&L, or income statement) shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, such as a month. A BALANCE SHEET shows, on one date, what the business owns (assets, like cash and equipment), what it owes (liabilities, like loans and unpaid bills), and the owner's equity: assets = liabilities + equity. A CASH FLOW statement shows where cash came from and went during a period. Each answers a different question.
questions.prompt: Which report shows profit over a month?

questions.correct_answer: The profit and loss statement

questions.section_skill: Using assets = liabilities + equity
questions.outcome_title: Tell what a profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow summary each show
questions.intro: The balance sheet equation is assets = liabilities + equity. If you know two of the numbers, you can find the third. To find equity: equity = assets - liabilities. To find assets: add liabilities and equity. Example: liabilities 3,000 and equity 5,000 means assets are 8,000. Check by adding back: if equity = assets - liabilities, then liabilities + equity must equal the assets you started with.

questions.outcome_title: Tell what a profit-and-loss statement, balance sheet and cash-flow summary each show
questions.intro: Three common reports summarize the books. A PROFIT AND LOSS statement (P&L, or income statement) shows revenue, expenses and profit over a period, such as a month. A BALANCE SHEET shows, on one date, what the business owns (assets, like cash and equipment), what it owes (liabilities, like loans and unpaid bills), and the owner's equity: assets = liabilities + equity. A CASH FLOW statement shows where cash came from and went during a period. Each answers a different question.
questions.prompt: A balance sheet shows cash 2,000, equipment 3,000, a loan of 1,500 and unpaid bills of 500. What is equity?
questions.correct_answer: 3,000 dollars

questions.section_skill: Explain how deductions and credits differ
questions.outcome_title: Tell a tax deduction from a tax credit, and explain that a deduction does not make a purchase free
questions.intro: Two tax words are often confused. A DEDUCTION lowers the income that tax is calculated on (taxable income). A CREDIT lowers the tax itself, dollar for dollar. Example with a made-up 20 percent rate: a 1,000-dollar deduction lowers taxable income by 1,000 and saves about 0.20 x 1,000 = 200 dollars of tax; a 1,000-dollar credit cuts the tax by 1,000 dollars. A credit applies only if the business is eligible, and some credits cannot reduce the tax below zero. Business expenses that are ordinary and necessary for the business are commonly deductible; which credits apply depends on current law, so check with a tax professional.

questions.outcome_title: Separate business and personal use of an item or account
questions.intro: Some items are used for both business and personal life: a car, a phone, a home internet plan, or part of a home. Generally only the BUSINESS-USE PORTION can be treated as a business expense. Keep evidence of the split: a mileage log for a car, or a reasonable record of phone use. Example: if a phone bill is 60 dollars and 40 percent of use is for business, the business portion is 0.40 x 60 = 24 dollars. Home office rules are specific; check official guidance or a tax professional.

questions.section_skill: Taking a share and keeping the rest
questions.outcome_title: Set aside a stated share of profit for taxes using an assumed rate
questions.intro: If you set aside a share of a payment, you keep the rest. Set aside = percent x payment; keep = payment - set aside. With 25 percent of 800: set aside 0.25 x 800 = 200, keep 800 - 200 = 600. Shortcut: keep = payment x (1 - percent) = 800 x 0.75 = 600. Check: 200 + 600 = 800. The two parts always add back to the full payment.

questions.section_skill: Write a clear quote with inclusions, exclusions and validity
questions.outcome_title: Write or judge a quote that states the work, price and what is not included
questions.intro: A QUOTE (or estimate) tells a customer what a job will cost before work begins. questions.section_skill: Recognize payment scams and verify before paying
questions.outcome_title: Spot fraud signals in invoices, overpayments and changed payment details
questions.intro: Small businesses are common targets for payment scams. FAKE INVOICES bill for things you never ordered, such as directory listings. CHANGED BANK DETAILS scams send an email that looks like a real supplier asking you to pay a new account. OVERPAYMENT scams send too much money (often by a check that later bounces) and ask you to send back the difference. Protection: match invoices to orders, confirm any bank-detail change by calling a known number (not one in the email), and never send back an "overpayment." A bank may make check funds available within days, yet the check can still be returned as fake weeks later, and the depositor owes the money.

questions.set_title: Domain, hosting and builders: who owns what
questions.section_skill: Know the parts of a website and who controls each
questions.outcome_title: Tell a domain, hosting and a website builder apart, and keep ownership, renewals and recovery access
questions.intro: A website has parts. The DOMAIN is the address (yourshop.example), rented yearly from a registrar. HOSTING is the service that stores the site and shows it to visitors. A WEBSITE BUILDER combines hosting and design tools. Check WHO OWNS each part: the domain should be registered in the business owner's name and account, not only a designer's. questions.section_skill: Use HTTPS, test key paths and keep tested backups
questions.outcome_title: Check HTTPS, test links, forms and checkout, and keep backups
questions.intro: HTTPS encrypts the connection between the visitor and the site; most builders and hosts provide it, often free. Browsers show it differently, and Chrome replaced its padlock with a settings icon, so check that the address starts with "https://" or open the browser's site information to see that the connection is secure. TEST before launch and after changes: click every link, submit every form, place a test order, and check on a phone. BACKUPS are copies of the site and its data; keep them regularly and know how to restore one. A backup you have never tested may not work when you need it.

questions.outcome_title: Improve how search engines and people understand a page, without promised rankings
questions.intro: SEARCH VISIBILITY means people can find your site when they search. questions.section_skill: Build an email list with permission and follow opt-out rules
questions.outcome_title: Build an email list with permission and honor unsubscribe requests
questions.intro: An EMAIL LIST lets you contact people who asked to hear from you. Build it with PERMISSION: a sign-up form where people choose to join. Under the US CAN-SPAM Act, commercial emails must not use misleading headers or subject lines, must tell recipients how to opt out, must honor opt-out requests, and must include a valid physical postal address (which can be a registered PO Box or private mailbox). The rules cover business-to-business email too. Buying lists of strangers' addresses damages trust and deliverability.

By buying a list of strangers' addresses online
With permission, through a sign-up form
By guessing addresses at popular email providers

questions.correct_answer: With permission, through a sign-up form

By buying a list of strangers' addresses online
By guessing addresses at popular email providers

questions.section_skill: Use real reviews with permission and avoid fake ones
questions.outcome_title: Use real testimonials with permission and ask for honest reviews
questions.intro: Reviews and testimonials are powerful because they come from customers, so they must be REAL. Ask customers for permission before quoting them, use their actual words (fixing only small typos), and do not show a review as typical if it is not. Never write fake reviews, pay for positive reviews, or use AI to invent customer experiences; the FTC treats fake reviews and testimonials as deceptive. Respond calmly and helpfully to negative reviews; do not threaten or pay reviewers to remove them.

questions.outcome_title: Compute and compare reach, leads, sales and conversion rates
questions.intro: Marketing results can be followed in steps. REACH is how many people saw your message. LEADS are people who showed interest, such as signing up or asking a question. SALES are people who paid. Each step has a CONVERSION RATE: leads / reach, and sales / leads. Example: 2,000 reached, 100 leads (5 percent), 20 sales (20 percent of leads). questions.intro: Consistency beats bursts. A CONTENT CALENDAR plans what to post and when, for example two useful posts a week on set days. questions.intro: A PROCEDURE (or checklist) writes down the steps for a task that repeats, such as opening the shop, packing an order, or closing out the day. questions.intro: INVENTORY is the stock of goods or materials you hold to sell. Too little and you run out; too much ties up cash and risks damage or items going out of style. A REORDER POINT tells you when to order more: reorder point = average daily use x lead time (days to arrive) + SAFETY STOCK (a small extra cushion). questions.outcome_title: Protect accounts with unique passwords, multifactor authentication and backups
questions.intro: Business accounts (bank, email, website, payment processor) are valuable targets. Basics: use a long, UNIQUE password for each account, stored in a PASSWORD MANAGER (a secure app that remembers passwords). Turn on TWO-STEP LOGIN (also called two-factor authentication), which asks for a second proof, such as a code from an app, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Keep BACKUPS of important files in a separate place and test that you can restore them. Be wary of messages asking for codes or passwords.

questions.intro: Insurance moves some financial risk to an insurer in exchange for a PREMIUM (the price of the policy). Common business categories include GENERAL LIABILITY (injuries or property damage to others, such as a customer slipping), PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY (mistakes in advice or services), PROPERTY (your equipment and inventory), and COMMERCIAL AUTO. Policy terms can include LIMITS (the most it pays), a DEDUCTIBLE (what you pay first on a covered claim), and EXCLUSIONS (what it does not cover). questions.set_title: Permission to use images, music, code and names
questions.section_skill: Get permission or a license for images, music, code and names
questions.outcome_title: Recognize copyright and trademark issues and get permission or use licensed material
questions.intro: Things you find online are usually owned by someone. Using another person's PHOTO, MUSIC, ARTWORK, written text or software CODE in your business generally needs PERMISSION, a LICENSE (written terms of use), or a source that clearly allows your kind of use. Public-domain works are free to use, and fair use is a narrow legal exception decided case by case; credit alone is not permission. "I found it on Google" is not permission. Read license terms: some allow only personal use, or require credit. Using another business's NAME or LOGO in a way that confuses customers can infringe trademark rights. Registering a business name, DBA or domain is not the same as trademark rights.

questions.intro: Whether a worker is an EMPLOYEE or an INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR depends on the actual working relationship, not on the label in a contract. Factors often include how much control the business has over how and when the work is done, whether the worker can profit or lose based on their own decisions, whether they work for other clients, who provides tools, and whether the work is ongoing. questions.intro: A service business sells time, so CAPACITY depends on how many appointments fit in a day. Count appointment length, TRAVEL between appointments, and a small BUFFER for delays. Example: a 9-hour day with 1.5-hour appointments plus 30 minutes of travel each fits 9 / 2 = 4.5, so 4 appointments. Grouping clients by area (ROUTING) reduces travel and increases capacity. Track no-shows and late cancellations, which waste capacity.

questions.section_skill: Activation and retention rates
questions.outcome_title: Help new users succeed and measure whether they keep using it
questions.intro: Rates compare a part to a whole. Activation = users who reached a first useful result / users who signed up. Retention at 30 days = users still active / users who started. Example: 80 sign up, 28 activate: 28 / 80 = 35 percent. If 14 are active after 30 days: 14 / 80 = 17.5 percent. Use the same starting group for both.
questions.prompt: 28 of 80 activate. What is the rate?
questions.correct_answer: 35 percent

questions.outcome_title: Use original or licensed material and respect others' rights
questions.intro: Content creators build on ORIGINAL work: your own writing, photos, video, music and ideas. To use someone else's clips, songs, images or text you need a valid legal basis: permission or a license, a public-domain work, or a legal exception such as fair use, which is decided case by case. Giving credit alone is not one of these. Some platforms have tools that detect copyrighted material and may block, mute or remove content. Keep records of licenses and permissions. If you film people, especially in private settings, get their permission to publish. Original work protects your channel and builds a distinct voice.
